scope.concept: The histogram shows when activity changed, so it can time an incident more exactly than a report can.
scope.narration: Support noticed the failures at ${incident.noticed_clock} (${incident.noticed_ago}), but not when they began. Find where the histogram rises above its usual level, then set the window to start just before that rise.
scope.reasoning: A window that starts just before the rise holds the whole incident, without older traffic mixed into the comparison.
scope.evidence: The histogram should show the raised stretch, with only a little normal traffic either side.

demonstration.narration: Support noticed the failures at ${incident.noticed_clock}, not when they began. Looking at the histogram, I can see the bars rise above the usual level, then fall back. I'll start at ${incident.window_start_clock}, just before the rise, and end at now.
demonstration.evidence: The histogram now starts at ${incident.window_start_clock}, just before the taller bars. It holds the whole rise, its fall back to the usual level, and some normal traffic on either side. That is probably the incident window. Next, I'll check the status codes to see whether the extra activity was failures.

hints: Support noticed the failures at ${incident.noticed_clock}, but they may have started earlier. Look for where the histogram rises above its usual level.
Click the date box at the top of Discover. Type a start date and time just before the rise, then “to now”. Or drag across the histogram.
Start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}: type “${incident.window_start_typed} to now”. Show me can do it for you.

isolate.title: Filter to the failing status code
isolate.concept: Filter on a value you actually saw in the data, not one you guessed. That leaves just the failing records.
isolate.narration: Filter for the status code that stood out in its Top values. Click the + next to it, or use Add filter. Only the failing requests should remain.
isolate.reasoning: This value comes from the Top values you just read, so the filter rests on evidence, not a guess. As its own filter pill, it is also easy to remove with one click, without editing any query text.
isolate.evidence: After you filter, the table and histogram show only the failing requests behind the incident.

demonstration.narration: I'll filter to ${param.incident.status} so the remaining requests show where the failures happened.
demonstration.reasoning:
The window still contains healthy 200s and other traffic.

Filtering for the ${param.incident.status} we saw in Top values leaves only the failing requests. As a separate filter pill, it is also easy to remove later.
demonstration.evidence: The hit count dropped to just the ${param.incident.status} responses, the failing requests. The filter sits under the query bar as a filter pill: the small box that reads ${var.status_field}: ${param.incident.status}. Its × removes the filter when you need the wider view again.

hints: Filter for the status code you just saw stand out, not one you assumed.
Click the + next to that value in the field's top values, or use Add filter (field, operator ‘is’, value).

demonstration.narration: I'll open one filtered request to check whether the unusual status and endpoint occur together.
demonstration.reasoning: A total can look convincing even when it includes other records. Opening one typical event shows the key values together, which a count alone can't do.
demonstration.evidence: This one request has both ${param.incident.status} and ${param.incident.route}. So the status and the endpoint really go together, not just in separate totals. ${truth.conclusion}

goal.title: Look at the status codes in the window
goal.concept: A field's Top values count every record in the window. So they show which value is unusual, which a few rows can't.
goal.narration: The table only shows a few requests at a time. Open the http.response.status_code field in the sidebar and read its Top values. They count the whole window, so they show which status code is unusual.
goal.reasoning: The report never named a status code, and the newest rows are only a sample. Reading the Top values keeps us honest instead of guessing.
goal.evidence: The field's top values show the unusual status code standing out from the healthy 200s.

demonstration.narration: The table lists single requests, newest first. I'll check status-code Top values to see which code stands out across the whole window.
demonstration.reasoning: A few rows can't show which code is most common, and filtering on a guess would assume the answer. Top values count every request in the window.
demonstration.evidence: The highlighted row is ${param.incident.status}, a server error with a large share of the window next to the healthy 200s. Top values counted every request, not just the rows on screen, so it's the value to filter on.

hints: Let the data show you which status code is unusual, instead of assuming one.
Open the http.response.status_code field in the sidebar and read its Top values (or add it as a column).

drifts.note: You opened ${action.field}; this step is about which status code stands out.

goal.title: Find the affected endpoint
goal.concept: Inside the failing requests, a second field's top values show where the failures are happening.
goal.narration: The failing status code is now filtered. Open the url.path field and read its Top values to see which endpoint the errors hit.
goal.reasoning: Knowing the status code isn't the same as knowing where it happens. The url.path top values show whether one route is behind most of them.
goal.evidence: The url.path top values show the endpoint behind all of the failures.

demonstration.narration: I'll check url.path Top values within the ${param.incident.status} responses to see which endpoint the failures hit.
demonstration.reasoning: The failures could be spread across many routes, or all on one. Reading url.path in the filtered results tells us which.
demonstration.evidence: All of the ${param.incident.status} responses are on ${param.incident.route}, which serves the ${param.incident.journey} requests that support said were failing. The failures are tied to that one endpoint, not spread across the API.

hints: Look at which endpoint the failing requests actually hit.

checks.title: Time range
checks.detail: We found when the failures started from the rise in the histogram, and set the time window around it.

checks.title: Status codes
checks.detail: We counted the status codes across the whole window and found the error code that stood out.

checks.title: Affected endpoint
checks.detail: We kept only the failing requests, and found that they were all on one endpoint.

checks.title: Confirming
checks.detail: We opened one failing request to confirm that the error and the endpoint go together.
